refs.1.1: Explain how the sub-cellular structures of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells are related to their functions, including: a animal cells – nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes b plant cells – nucleus, cell membrane, cell wall, chloroplasts, mitochondria, vacuole and ribosomes c bacteria – chromosomal DNA, plasmid DNA, cell membrane, ribosomes and flagella

refs.1.3: Explain how changes in microscope technology, including electron microscopy, have enabled us to see cell structures and organelles with more clarity and detail than in the past and increased our understanding of the role of sub-cellular structures
refs.1.4: Demonstrate an understanding of number, size and scale, including the use of estimations and explain when they should be used
refs.1.5: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between quantitative units in relation to cells, including: a milli (10 ) b micro (10 ) c nano (10 ) d pico (10 ) e calculations with numbers written in standard form

refs.1.14B: Explain how the energy contained in food can be measured using calorimetry

refs.2.1: Describe mitosis as part of the cell cycle, including the stages interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase and cytokinesis
refs.2.2: Describe the importance of mitosis in growth, repair and asexual reproduction

refs.2.4: Describe cancer as the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division
refs.2.5: Describe growth in organisms, including: a cell division and differentiation in animals b cell division, elongation and differentiation in plants
refs.2.6: Explain the importance of cell differentiation in the development of specialised cells
refs.2.7: Demonstrate an understanding of the use of percentiles charts to monitor growth

refs.2.11B: Explain how the difficulties of accessing brain tissue inside the skull can be overcome by using CT scanning and PET scanning to investigate brain function
refs.2.12B: Explain some of the limitations in treating damage and disease in the brain and other parts of the nervous system, including spinal injuries and brain tumours
refs.2.13: Explain the structure and function of sensory receptors, sensory neurones, relay neurones in the CNS, motor neurones and synapses in the transmission of electrical impulses, including the axon, dendron, myelin sheath and the role of neurotransmitters
refs.2.14: Explain the structure and function of a reflex arc including sensory, relay and motor neurones 14

refs.2.17B: Explain how cataracts, long-sightedness and short-sightedness can be corrected
refs.3.1B: Explain some of the advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction, including the lack of need to find a mate, a rapid reproductive cycle, but no variation in the population
refs.3.2B: Explain some of the advantages and disadvantages of sexual reproduction, including variation in the population, but the requirement to find a mate
refs.3.3: Explain the role of meiotic cell division, including the production of four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes, and that this results in the formation of genetically different haploid gametes The stages of meiosis are not required
refs.3.4: Describe DNA as a polymer made up of: a two strands coiled to form a double helix b strands linked by a series of complementary base pairs joined together by weak hydrogen bonds c nucleotides that consist of a sugar and phosphate group with one of the four different bases attached to the sugar

refs.3.6: Explain how DNA can be extracted from fruit

refs.4.1B: Describe the work of Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace in the development of the theory of evolution by natural selection and explain the impact of these ideas on modern biology
refs.4.2: Explain Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection
refs.4.3: Explain how the emergence of resistant organisms supports Charles Darwin's theory of evolution including antibiotic resistance in bacteria

refs.5.1: Describe health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO)
refs.5.2: Describe the difference between communicable and non-communicable diseases
refs.5.3: Explain why the presence of one disease can lead to a higher susceptibility to other diseases
refs.5.4: Describe a pathogen as a disease-causing organism, including viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists
refs.5.5: Describe some common infections, including: a cholera (bacteria) causes diarrhoea b tuberculosis (bacteria) causes lung damage c Chalara ash dieback (fungi) causes leaf loss and bark lesions d malaria (protists) causes damage to blood and liver e HIV (virus) destroys white blood cells, leading to the onset of AIDS fB stomach ulcers caused by Helicobacter (bacteria) gB Ebola (virus) causes haemorrhagic fever
refs.5.6: Explain how pathogens are spread and how this spread can be reduced or prevented, including: a cholera (bacteria) – water b tuberculosis (bacteria) – airborne c Chalara ash dieback (fungi) – airborne d malaria (protists) – animal vectors eB stomach ulcers caused by Helicobacter (bacteria) – oral transmission fB Ebola (virus) – body fluids
refs.5.7B: Describe the lifecycle of a virus, including lysogenic and lytic pathways

refs.5.15B: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of immunisation, including the concept of herd immunity
